title: Register space of obstruction-free set agreement
formal: For every integer pair \(n>k\ge1\), determine \(R(n,k)\), the minimum number of shared atomic read/write registers sufficient for deterministic obstruction-free one-shot \(k\)-set agreement among \(n\) named processes with input domain \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), in the model below. Supply a real-valued function approximating \(R\) with pointwise absolute error at most \(1/100\) registers throughout this domain.
definitions:
Fix \(n>k\ge1\). There are \(n\) processes with distinct known identifiers \(1,\ldots,n\); each knows \(n,k\) and initially knows only its own input in \([n]\), not other processes' inputs. A protocol may depend on \(n,k\), and is given by finite deterministic programs with unbounded private storage and no bound on finite local computation. No uniform procedure generating protocols for different \(n,k\) is required. A process may invoke the task at most once; it participates when it invokes, and may decide at most once, after which it stops. Any subset may participate.

The only communication is through a fixed array of \(r\ge0\) shared multiwriter/multireader registers with common names \(1,\ldots,r\). Every process can read and write every register. A register stores a finite binary string of unrestricted length; one atomic read returns its entire current string, and one atomic write replaces that string. Initial shared contents may depend on \(n,k\) and the protocol but are fixed independently of the input assignment and participation. All shared storage is in these counted registers. A scheduled process takes a local computation step, including invocation or decision, or performs one atomic read or write with a finite local update; no stronger shared primitive, random choice, clock, or failure detector is supplied.

An execution is any finite or infinite interleaving of such steps; a process may stop forever at any point, representing a crash, with no fairness or timing assumption. In every finite execution prefix, each decided value must be the input proposed by a process that has already invoked, and at most \(k\) distinct values may have been decided.

Obstruction-freedom requires that, from every reachable configuration, every participating undecided process \(p\) decides after finitely many further own steps if only \(p\) is scheduled thereafter. Other processes may subsequently resume, so safety must also hold under every extension. Register widths, private storage and running time are uncharged.

Define \(R(n,k)\) as the least integer \(r\) for which a protocol satisfies these requirements for every assignment of inputs and every schedule. A finite sufficient \(r\) is known, so this minimum exists.
why: This measures how much shared memory is intrinsically needed for synchronization when processes may disagree on a bounded number of proposed values. Resolving the gap would connect the solvability of agreement tasks to their exact memory requirements, even under the weak guarantee of eventual progress in isolation.

context_blocks.text: The known bounds are \(\lceil n/k\rceil\le R(n,k)\le n-k+1\). The lower bound applies to named processes; the upper bound is achieved even by anonymous processes, so it also applies here. Both ends of the parameter range are determined: \(R(n,1)=n\) and \(R(n,n-1)=2\). In the interior, the general bounds can leave a substantial gap.

The upper-bound algorithm uses exactly \(n-k+1\) physical read/write registers, including the implementation of the snapshots appearing in its presentation. The resource is the number of arbitrarily large registers, not their combined bit capacity. The repeated version, in which processes solve a sequence of agreement instances, already has the exact bound \(n-k+1\); this card concerns one invocation per process.

Ellen, Gelashvili and Zhu conjecture in the preprint that the exact register requirement for \(x\)-obstruction-free \(k\)-set agreement is \(n-k+x\), for \(1\le x\le k<n\). Here \(x\)-obstruction-freedom means that all sufficiently active processes finish whenever at most \(x\) processes continue taking steps. The present question fixes \(x=1\) and asks for the full optimal function, an editorial broadening of the resulting conjecture \(R(n,k)=n-k+1\). It also accepts a determination that refutes that conjecture.

The OPODIS 2025 paper published in January 2026 still lists the same lower and upper bounds for the n-valued problem. Its results about different wait-free tasks do not close this gap. Bounds for swap or other stronger shared objects concern different computational models.

A second paper published in January 2026 continues to state the same register-space bounds while studying limitations of particular classes of impossibility proofs. It does not determine the register-space function.

references.title: Anonymous Obstruction-Free \((n,k)\)-Set Agreement with \(n-k+1\) Atomic Read/Write Registers
references.authors: Zohir Bouzid; Michel Raynal; Pierre Sutra

references.title: Solving Tasks with Fewer Registers Than Processes
references.authors: Eli Gafni; Giuliano Losa; Michel Raynal; Gadi Taubenfeld
references.locator: OPODIS 2025, article 21, published 7 January 2026. Section 2, p. 21:3: deterministic unbounded-state processes, unbounded-size MRMW registers and process/register anonymity. Section 7, p. 21:15: lower and upper bounds for n-valued x-obstruction-free k-set agreement; p. 21:16 distinguishes stronger base objects. The main new results concern different wait-free tasks.

references.title: How Exhaustive Does an Extension-Based Proof Need to Be?
references.authors: Faith Ellen; Shihao Liu; Leqi Zhu; Eli Gafni; Rati Gelashvili
references.locator: OPODIS 2025, article 29, published 7 January 2026. Section 5, p. 29:17, still states the n/k-register lower bound and n-k+1-register upper bound for obstruction-free k-set agreement. Its new results concern limits on classes of impossibility proofs, not a determination of register space.

progress.text: Bouzid, Raynal and Sutra give an anonymous obstruction-free one-shot protocol using \(n-k+1\) atomic read/write registers. Their repeated-task extension has the already optimal repeated-task register count.

The revisionist-simulation preprint establishes the lower bound \(\lfloor(n-x)/(k+1-x)\rfloor+1\) for \(1\le x\le k<n\). At \(x=1\) this equals \(\lceil n/k\rceil\); the preprint also states the conjecture that the upper bound is exact.
The journal publication states the \(\lceil n/k\rceil\) obstruction-free register lower bound and describes determining the required number of registers as open.
The published OPODIS 2025 related-work account retains the lower/upper gap for n-valued obstruction-free set agreement.
The paper on exhaustive extension-based proofs also retains these register bounds; its main theorems address proof-system limitations rather than a new register-space bound.

answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously specified real-valued function \(g\) on all integer pairs \(n>k\ge1\), and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|g(n,k)-R(n,k)|\le1/100\) throughout the domain, with error measured in registers and \(R\) defined by the stated model. The approximation need not be integer-valued. A certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies through its midpoint. Exact determination also qualifies. A finite table, an asymptotic estimate, or unmatched bounds outside this precision do not meet the criterion; merely restating the defining minimization does not specify a determination.
status_note: The 2024 journal abstract explicitly describes determining register space as open. Two primary papers published on 7 January 2026 retain the same general bounds. A bounded primary-source and subsequent-result review through 16 September 2026 found no verified determination for all \(n>k\ge1\); this is not exhaustive certification of current openness. The 1/100 tolerance is the atlas acceptance rule, not a tolerance proposed by these papers.

importance.reason: This measures a basic memory cost of synchronization and exposes a large gap between known impossibility arguments and protocols.

category_assignment.reason: Asynchronous task solvability and shared-register complexity are distributed-computing questions.

sentences: Each process proposes a value and must decide one of the values proposed by participating processes.
At most k distinct values may be decided, and a process must finish if it continues alone long enough.
The resource is the number of atomic read/write registers, whose individual capacities are unrestricted.
Known bounds range from the ceiling of n/k to n-k+1; consensus and (n-1)-set agreement have exact values.
The target is the full register-space function for all n>k>=1, with the atlas's pointwise 1/100-register acceptance tolerance.
